17.explain: D: Lindqvist's warning about drinking far beyond thirst, which can dilute blood sodium — more runners harmed by too much water than too little.
17.evidence: more runners are harmed by too much water than by too little

18.explain: F: decades of results show the fastest marathons happen on cool, still days around ten to twelve degrees.
18.evidence: marathons are fastest on cool, still days at around ten to twelve degrees Celsius

19.explain: Glycogen is defined in the same sentence as the fuel made from carbohydrate, stored in muscles and liver.
19.evidence: glycogen, the fuel made from carbohydrate, in its muscles and liver

20.explain: When glycogen runs low the body switches fuel, and the replacement demands more oxygen per stride — which is why the pace collapses.
20.evidence: the body turns to burning fat, a fuel that demands more oxygen for every stride

21.explain: Ochieng's point is that the brakes are neurological, not muscular: the brain reads the fuel gauge and refuses to let the legs be emptied.
21.evidence: The brain reads the fuel gauge and applies the brakes before real damage is done

22.explain: His unglamorous defence is an even pace from the first kilometre, however fresh the legs feel.
22.evidence: an even pace from the first kilometre, however fresh the legs feel

23.explain: A: Lindqvist's advice is to drink when thirsty and no more. E inverts her other advice — she says to eat plenty of carbohydrate beforehand — and B is what elites do about engine size, not advice for ordinary runners.
23.evidence: and on the day itself drink when thirsty, and no more

24.explain: C: the even pace, given twice — by Ochieng in paragraph C and again in the closing summary of 'almost comic modesty'.
24.evidence: run an even pace, and drink when you are thirsty

25.explain: B: the measured figure is about four per cent. A is wrong — a ban was demanded but the governing body set limits instead — and E is wrong because the muscle-damage claim rests on much weaker evidence.
25.evidence: an improvement in running economy of about four per cent

26.explain: D: Soto led one of the laboratory teams and measured the effect on treadmill runners. C is contradicted in the same paragraph — the benefit varies noticeably between individuals.
26.evidence: led one of the laboratory teams that measured the effect on treadmill runners

27.explain: B: a couple of dozen giant languages are spoken by half of humanity while thousands survive in single valleys or families. The writer also warns that the 'one every few weeks' claim deserves caution, so D is wrong.
27.evidence: but the figure conceals an extraordinary imbalance

28.explain: D: the writer explicitly corrects the popular image — languages are rarely lost because speakers die out, and prohibition is not the usual cause. It is a chain of private decisions about what to speak to children.
28.evidence: Far more often, a language dies through a long chain of private decisions

29.explain: A: the writer says outright that the point is not exoticism but range — the human mind has more settings than any one language shows.
29.evidence: but that the human mind has more settings than any single language reveals

30.explain: C: 'Technology cuts both ways here.' The phone pours dominant languages into every pocket and is also the cheapest recording studio ever made.

31.explain: YES: the writer questions how free the choice is when one language carries prestige and schooling and the other carries stigma — 'weighted long before any parent makes it'.
31.evidence: Language shift is less like a preference and more like surrender to pressure

32.explain: NOT GIVEN: the passage contrasts documentation with revival as activities, but says nothing about government spending on either.
32.evidence: Documentation, however, is not revival, and the distinction matters

33.explain: NO: the seed image makes the point precisely — an archived language is safe but not growing.
33.evidence: An archived language is like a preserved seed: safe, but not growing

34.explain: YES: linguists supplied materials and schools helped, but the writer places the decisive act in kitchens rather than universities.
34.evidence: but the decisive act took place in kitchens, not in universities

35.explain: NO: the writer calls this a false choice. Human beings are built for bilingualism, and keeping a grandmother's tongue costs nothing of a global one.
35.evidence: a child who keeps a grandmother's tongue loses no part of a global one

36.explain: F, pressure. The summary compresses the second paragraph, where the writer rejects 'preference' in favour of surrender to social and economic pressure.
36.evidence: Language shift is less like a preference and more like surrender to pressure

37.explain: E, experiment. Every language is called a natural experiment in what a human mind can do, and the diversity of the sample is the data.
37.evidence: Every language is a natural experiment in what a human mind can do

38.explain: A, archives. The recordings are transcribed and archived, and the passage closes by urging that the archives be filled urgently.
38.evidence: The archives should be filled, urgently, while the last speakers can still be recorded

39.explain: H, recordings. Field linguists now aim to capture living speech — stories, arguments, songs, jokes — not word lists.
39.evidence: aiming to capture not word lists but living speech: stories, arguments, songs, jokes

40.explain: B, children. The passage's final test of a living language is a child hearing it from a parent and answering back.
40.evidence: A language lives when a child hears it from a parent and answers back
